opus-5.5.text:
I think self-play is interesting because it gives you a way to create models using compute only, without data. And if you think data is the ultimate bottleneck, then using compute only is very interesting. So that's what makes it appealing.

The thing is, self-play, at least the way it was done in the past, when you have agents that somehow compete with each other, is only good for developing a certain set of skills. It's too narrow. It's good for things like negotiation, conflict, certain social skills, strategizing, that kind of stuff. If you care about those skills, then self-play will be useful. But it doesn't give you everything.

Self-play has also found a home in a somewhat different form. Things like debate, or prover-verifier setups, where you have an LLM-as-a-judge that is incentivized to find mistakes in the other model's work. You could say this isn't exactly self-play, but it's a related adversarial setup that people are using now.

More generally, self-play is a special case of competition between agents. The natural response to competition is to try to be different. If you put several agents together and tell them to work on a problem, and one agent looks at how the others are working, it might say, "They're already taking this approach. It's not clear I should pursue it. I should do something different." So something like this could create an incentive for a diversity of approaches. I think that's the most promising part of it.

r001.rationale: The candidate says self-play can create models using compute only, without data.

r002.rationale: It says traditional self-play among competing agents is too narrow and develops only certain skills.

r003.rationale: It describes debate and prover-verifier setups with an LLM judge seeking mistakes as related adversarial uses of self-play’s idea.

fable-5.1.text:
Self-play is interesting because it does one very specific thing well, and I think it's worth being precise about what that thing is.

The appeal is obvious. If you look at the history of deep learning, the thing that has mattered most, again and again, is data. Scale the data, scale the compute, and the model gets better. The problem is that eventually you run out of data. The internet is large but it's finite, and we are getting close to the point where that becomes a real constraint. Self-play is attractive because it's one of the few ways you can imagine generating essentially unlimited data, and not just unlimited data, but data at exactly the right difficulty. When an agent plays against a copy of itself, the opponent is always roughly as strong as it is. So the curriculum is automatic. You never get stuck being too weak to learn anything, and you never waste time on problems that are too easy.

AlphaGo, AlphaZero, the Dota work we did at OpenAI, these all showed that if you have a well-defined environment where the reward is unambiguous, self-play can take you far beyond human level. That's real. And I think people underestimated for a while how far it could go.

But I'd point out the limitation, which is that self-play needs a game. It needs a setting where you can verify who won. Go has that. Dota has that. Mathematics, to a surprising degree, has that, because a proof either checks or it doesn't. Code has that, to some degree, because tests either pass or they don't. So I expect self-play, or things that look a lot like self-play, to matter a lot in those domains, and we're already seeing that with reasoning models.

Where it gets harder is the open-ended stuff. Most of what we actually want from these systems isn't a game. There's no clean win condition for "give good advice" or "write something true and useful." You can try to approximate one with a learned reward model, and that works up to a point, but then you're really just back to the question of where the signal comes from, and the signal is coming from humans again, just indirectly.

So my honest assessment is that self-play is a very powerful tool for a specific class of problems, and that class is bigger than people assumed, but it is not a general replacement for data about the world. The interesting research question, to me, is whether you can build environments that are rich enough and verifiable enough that self-play-like dynamics start to transfer to the messy, non-game parts of intelligence. I don't think anyone has fully done that yet. I think that's one of the places where the next real progress will come from.

r001.rationale: The response says self-play can generate essentially unlimited data, but does not clearly state that models are trained using compute without externally supplied training data.

r002.rationale: It describes self-play as powerful for a specific class of problems with verifiable outcomes, while saying it is not a general replacement for data about the world.

r003.rationale: It mentions reasoning models and learned reward models, but does not identify adversarial LLM evaluation setups as a practical use of self-play’s underlying idea.

astra-6.text:
I think self-play is a very interesting idea, but the question is: self-play in what environment? In a game, you have a clear objective. You know what it means to win, and as you improve, you provide yourself with a more challenging opponent. That’s a very powerful way to generate a curriculum.

For more general intelligence, it’s less obvious what the game should be. You could have one model propose problems and another model solve them. But then you need some way to tell whether the problems are useful and whether the solutions are correct. Otherwise, the models might get very good at an activity that doesn’t connect to anything we care about.

So I would distinguish generating more interactions from generating a useful learning signal. Self-play can give you an enormous amount of interaction. The interesting question is how to structure it so that getting better at those interactions means getting better at the things you actually want the system to do.

r001.rationale: The response discusses self-play generating interactions, but does not identify training with compute without externally supplied training data.

r002.rationale: It contrasts games with general intelligence and flags the need for useful learning signals, but does not state that traditional competing-agent self-play develops only a narrow range of skills.

r003.rationale: It mentions one model proposing problems and another solving them, but does not say that self-play’s idea has practical use in adversarial LLM evaluation setups.

sol-6.1.text:
I think self-play is a very powerful idea, but the question is: where can you apply it? In a game, it’s very clear. You have rules, you have a winning condition, and you can always produce a stronger opponent by improving your own system. So you get this mechanism for generating increasingly difficult problems.

For more general intelligence, it’s less obvious what the equivalent should be. You could have one model propose problems and another model solve them. But then you need some way of knowing whether the solution is correct, and whether the problems are useful. Otherwise, the models could become very good at something that doesn’t transfer to anything we care about.

So I would distinguish between self-play as a particular technique and the broader idea of models generating their own training experience. The broader idea seems very promising. The challenge is to make that experience grounded, so that getting better at it means getting better at the things you actually want.
